To be honest I don't understand what I'm getting in return for the additional indirection and reduction in clarity.

> To be honest I don't understand what I'm getting in return for the additional indirection and reduction in clarity.

Based on your concern i can go into detail here 😊

Let me know your thoughts on my response and we can go into detail on individual points 👍

What you get:

### no more typo or manual comparing

It's impossible to have a typo when using object paths, interface names and bus names  from the generated header.

### easier to review

When reviewing both new and old code there is less need to look at the PDI documentation for a given interface. Since we are using the symbol from the generated header.

It can lead to reduced number of iterations for development of new code.

For example consider someone creating an `xyz.openbmc_project.Sensor.Value` interface on `/xyz/openbmc_project/sensor/temperature/`.

Is it not `/xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/temperature/` ?
Or just plain `/xyz/openbmc_project/sensors/` ?

One would have to check back with the PDI yaml to see what the namespaces are.
When using the generated header it's easier to confirm 'at a glance' that the code is as expected.

### improved failure mode

When PDI interfaces are refactored or default bus names, object paths and interface names change, code using the generated header will get a compilation error.

Code using hardcoded string literals for bus names, interfaces, ... will simply fail at runtime.

This failure mode thing has special relevance for the error path which may be run infrequently. It may also be hard to test or changed without testing, or simply forgotten about code.

### improved refactoring capability

When PDI is implemented throughout, bus names, object path namespaces and interface names can be changed in a single patch on the PDI. When hardcoding approach is used, such changes result in lots of patches and needs gerrit topics and synchronized SRCREV bumping which can be tedious.

### on the indirection (in bus names)

Usually i don't care much about the specific bus name which is used.
If i want to debug using busctl, easy enough to look that up in the PDI.

It's a small step to look that up for a developer.
Depending on your IDE/Editor you could probably just go-to-definition on a given symbol.

### on the indirection (in interface names)

Similarly i don't care as much about the specific interface name. If it's 
`xyz.openbmc_project.Item.Cpu` or `xyz.openbmc_project.Item.CPU`
or `xyz.Item.Cpu`.

- the prefix is redundant for the understanding, it's just namespacing and not super valuable for the reader
- for the suffix e.g. `Item.Cpu` i usually want to know if it actually exists.

I did have a small number of encounters with properties and interfaces that did not actually exist in the PDI.

When using generated headers there is no such worry since these things come from the header and we can be sure that the interface / property actually exists and is not some forgotten relic.

### improved code search for properties and method names

When using-directivo `using SensorValue = ...`
is applied then we can look for 
`SensorValue::property_names::value` instead of `"Value"`.

Otherwise, property `Value` is part of following other interfaces also
- Metric.Value
- Common.Threshold
- State.Boot.Raw

Since the PDI is properly namespaced, we can use the namespaces for a better code search.

Sorry I didn't respond.  I have the same opposing opinions that have been voiced elsewhere by others previously in places like entity-manager and dbus-sensors.  I don't see any point in rehashing them yet again.
I think I know what it is but I'd be keen to get my co-maintainers opinion here @spinler@us.ibm.com.

The issue here I suppose is that this repo uses the async functions and so there is no need for PDI other than these constants.

I can live with that rule, I know people feel strongly about this stuff.

The true downside I see is that it comes from generated code and so you can't find it browsing github and you have to compile first.
I find this to be worse from 'at a glance comprehension of what I'm looking at' than what we had before...

Thanks for your feedback here, but in this instance (with -10/+10 lines of context)
i would prefer the right side.

`xyz.openbmc_project.ObjectMapper` is a service name as well as a DBus interface name and using the qualified symbol name clarifies that the key in 'connectionMap' is a `service name`.

It is not typed any better than before but the symbol name (and its namespace) provide additional context which can help with understanding.

Maybe you are looking at this from the perspective of someone new to openbmc.

In which case i would recommend them to use the LSP support of their editor to go-to-definition to see the value behind that symbol.

Because you already know what's the default service name for object mapper, i do not see how it would be worse for you personally?

From a D-Bus programming point of view, the words 'default service name' are nonsensical.  Service names define what interfaces exist.  The mapper interface is always implemented by the mapper service, regardless of the implementation in use.  I don't particularly care to see non-sensical symbol names in the code.

In general I would like to see OpenBMC evolve towards more traditional D-Bus programming semantics.

Using the same constant from the same header in both the client and the server seems like a good thing to me, so that they are guaranteed to match.  That's the point of this.  You can't use 'default_service' on just any interface, just a case like here where you can't look it up in the mapper. (I think also logging uses it).

I already mentioned above though why I can understand not wanting it in this repo.
